scores.note: Her eye flares into a bright bar, she rocks back, freezes for half a second, tiptoes backwards and then whips round with a springy overshoot. It's clean and the weight feels right. But at TV size the recoil is only a few pixels, so it reads as a pause with a bright eye, and only whoever is watching Maya closely gets the "she saw us!" laugh.

On screen it's almost the same take as 1a, plus Theo turning to watch her and back. That's too small to notice from the couch, and for about a second Theo looks as if he faces east when he really faces south. It also adds the most time of the three, about 1.3 s over today's pace.

The loudest of the three. A crash zoom with a white lens streak, then the room goes black until only her eye glows and blinks, then it all snaps back as she whips north. It will get a big laugh the first time. But eyes blinking in the dark is a stock cartoon gag, the board and Theo vanish for about a second, and the U-Turn starts while the screen is still dark. Four or five blackouts a game would wear thin fast.

A big claw of light bounces down its line, grips her, strains, carries her north swinging like a real pendulum, and drops her with a pink shock ring on the glass. It's huge, it reads from any seat, and it's a Move Back the room will ask to see again. Three flaws: the slip before the drop barely shows, the claw is so bright it blooms over Maya while she's in its grip, and the fingers flail into a squiggle as it reels up.

The classic three-pronged arcade claw is the clearest shape in the set, and Maya sells it. She looks up and squashes (a gulp), dangles high with her ring left on the floor, lands with a bounce, glares, and does the U-Turn with her nose in the air. The one blemish is Theo: when he looks up, his prism tips into the glass and for a moment looks like broken shards.

The most Lumen staging. The room dims to one warm lamp and a plumb line of amber light, and the slow-motion wobble over the spot is real suspense. But the camera leans in, which crops Theo and makes the one-space carry hard to follow. This claw is also small and sits on her like a crown, so "arcade claw" doesn't land as instantly as in 2a or 2b.

The splash, the flop and the dog-style shake-off land as comedy, and you clearly see her go under. But the "water" is a few wobbly white lines scribbled over one cell, the rings and beads make the frame busy, she's under for only about half a second, and the Rotate Right card arrives while she's still shaking.

The deep breath, the soft red glow sliding under the glass and the barrel-roll breach are sweet. But two artifacts stay on screen: a red dash at the dive point, and after she surfaces, a thin red line from her to the front edge of the board that lasts through the U-Turn. Theo's peering also twists his prism into an odd shape.

The real gasp among the dolphins. The camera sinks to the waterline and she breaches in slow motion trailed by strobe ghosts, with a lovely glow inside the slab. But the program card is pushed off the top of the frame for about a second, the ghosts briefly read as extra robots, and you can't tell where she'll land until the camera settles.

The curl on the turn, the shiver when Move Back pulls it, and the loop and bow on the U-Turn are charming, and they record her turns. But Theo turns to face her as a judge for about 3 s, which misreports his facing on the most common moment in the game. The pose and nod add about 0.6 s to every U-Turn, and the shiver looks more like an electrical zigzag than a ribbon.

The prettiest everyday entry. A soft, light-painted ribbon flicks a curl on the turn, cracks taut on Move Back and ties a glowing bow at her feet, all at today's pace. "She turned here" reads from the couch, and it will still be a small pleasure on the 100th card. The catch: when the ribbon is tugged straight, it runs diagonally from the curl to her, so the trail no longer shows the right-angle path she drove.

A clever idea, and the springy unwind after the U-Turn is satisfying. From the couch, though, the throttle tilt looks like the card being squashed into a sliver that hides its arrow, and the hand-over-hand spin adds about 0.5 s to every U-Turn.

More acting than 5a: a squat and launch, a reversing blink, dizzy sparkles after the U-Turn. But it adds about 1.3 s to this four-card program, which is too much for a moment this common, and the dizzy beat would be old by round two. A clipped half-dome of light around her on Move Back looks like a glitch, and Theo turns away for a second.

A thin control line with a bead of light running down it ties the card to its robot, and it keeps today's exact pace, so it could run all night. But it's gentle enough that most of the room won't notice it. As the card hands off to the tilting plane, a grey double of it shows for a few frames.

winner.why: The claw is the moment the couch shouts "again!". Everyone knows an arcade claw, so the second it lowers out of the dark the whole room is in on the joke, and the wobble over the spot is real suspense: arcade claws drop things. 2b is the clearest claw of the three, a classic three-pronged shape. Maya's reactions (the look up and gulp, the dangle, the glare, the nose-in-the-air U-Turn) turn it into a tiny story without moving the camera. It also follows the rule to the letter: one space back, still facing south, ending exactly on (3, 1) at 4.13 s, inside the 4.5 s budget.
winner.port: Theo's look-up: it tips his prism into the glass so it reads as broken. Drop it, or limit bystanders to a brief turn. Better still, keep other robots still, because their facing is game state the room reads. Rarity: keep it once or twice a game, seeded, and only on a Move Back with clear air above and an empty destination. Never give it to the same player twice in a row. Borrow from 2a: take the pendulum swing on the carry and the pink shock ring on landing. The ring gives the drop a punchline that reads from the back of the room. Light: keep the claw in Lumen's warm white, and check the bloom doesn't wash out the robot's colour while she's gripped. Trail and register: draw no trail for the carried space, as now. If several robots play Move Back in the same register, only one gets the claw. Keep the Move Back card visible throughout, as now, since it carries the rule.

runner_up.why: The same laugh with more weight. The claw bounces on its line and strains as she comes off the glass, she swings under it like a real pendulum, and the drop rings the glass with a shock ring that reads from anywhere in the room. 2b has the better-acting robot and 2a the better-feeling machine. Either would get the "again!".
runner_up.port: The slip: make the slip before the drop readable (a visible drop of a few pixels, then the catch), or cut it. At TV size it doesn't show. Brightness: pull the claw from white-hot to Lumen's warm white and cut the bloom, so Maya's red stays visible in the grip. Reel-up: keep the fingers rigid as the claw reels up. Right now they flail into a squiggle. Time: at 4.40 s it's right at the 4.5 s budget, so trim the hover rather than the drop.
